name: guard-clause
intent: Reject invalid input, impossible state and failed preconditions at the top of a callable with an immediate exit - return, throw, break or trap - so the remaining body runs only on the happy path and stays flat.
problem: A function that validates as it goes buries its normal path inside nested conditionals: every check adds a level of indentation around the work that follows, the else branch becomes the real body, and a failure discovered halfway down surfaces far from the input that caused it. The recurring decision is where the negative cases go - wrapped around the happy path, or pushed in front of it as prerequisites that exit immediately.
context: Applies inside function and method bodies in any paradigm: argument checks on public entry points and constructors, request handlers, parsers and deserialisers, worker loops, and C functions that must release resources on failure. The pattern is local to one callable - the decision it settles is how that body is shaped - so it composes with, rather than replaces, signature-level error contracts (Result, Option, Either, exceptions) and with boundary-level validation layers.
benefits: The happy path keeps one indentation level: each precondition is stated, exited and forgotten, so the code that does the work reads top to bottom without else-branch wrappers.
Failures are stated where they are caused: the requirement sits next to the value it protects instead of a nested branch deciding late whether the state was ever legal.
Each guard is a single, named, testable case - empty id, out of range, not ready - and maps one-to-one onto tests and error messages.
Separation of validation from processing: the guards form a visible admission band at the top, so it is obvious what a function accepts before any state changes or resources are acquired.
Cheap and tool-friendly: there is no structure to build or wire, and linters can enforce the shape mechanically (ESLint no-else-return, RuboCop Style/GuardClause).
tradeoffs: Multiple exit points: a long function with many guards becomes a list of diverging branches, and teams that rely on single-exit discipline for cleanup must route every exit through the same release path (a goto chain, defer, or finally) or leak - CERT MEM12-C documents exactly this leak in C.

Negated conditions read worse than positive ones: a guard states what must not hold, so compound checks readily become double negatives and De Morgan mistakes at precisely the place the failure logic must be right.

Scattered validation: one precondition per function, repeated in each caller, duplicates the rule and can fail open when one copy is updated and another is not; a boundary-level validator exists for that case.

Silent exits hide errors: a guard that returns a default (null, None, 0, empty collection) turns an invalid input into an ordinary-looking result and discards the reason; when failure must travel with the value, Result/Either/Option carry it and the guard is the wrong shape.
Position matters more than the check: validating early against state that changes before use creates time-of-check to time-of-use gaps, while validating late lets work happen before the rejection.

Readability can invert: in a function whose guards outnumber its work the code reads as mostly error handling, at which point extraction (Composed Method) or one dedicated validation step is the honest fix.
use_cases: Public API, command-handler and constructor entry points: reject null, empty and out-of-range arguments before any state changes, so a failure cannot leave partial work behind.
Deserialisers and parser steps: exit with None/Err at the first unparseable token instead of threading a validity flag through the rest of the parse.
Worker and event loops: a continue guard skips items that fail preconditions without indenting the processing body inside another conditional.
C functions that acquire several resources: argument guards before the first acquisition, then goto-chain exits for the failures that occur while resources are held (CERT MEM12-C).

Server request handling: cheap format and authentication checks at the top of the handler, leaving business logic at the top indentation level (pairs with Intercepting Validator when the same band repeats across handlers).
Test fixtures and doubles: guard the arrange step with explicit assumptions so a test fails loudly instead of exercising a degenerate object.

Cloud event handlers (AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Cloudflare Workers): guard at the top of the handler before any SDK call or I/O, ensuring no partial state is committed when a precondition fails and the response is short-circuited.

Middleware and edge computing pipelines: each middleware stage acts as a guard that either passes (await next()) or returns a terminal Response immediately (auth rejection, rate-limit exceeded), short-circuiting the chain before downstream handlers run.
Data pipeline transforms: schema-conformance guards check record shape before expensive field-level transformations, failing the entire step fast rather than producing malformed output.
gRPC and service-to-service RPC entry: proto-validated input guards run before any business logic in the handler, rejecting malformed or unauthorised requests with the appropriate status code.
Swift's guard statement (introduced in Swift 2): Apple requires its else branch to transfer control out of the scope, so optional bindings and preconditions stay available to the flat happy path.
Rust's ? operator and let-else: the Rust Reference documents error propagation and diverging pattern guards that return Err or None before later work executes.
ASP.NET Core middleware: a component can short-circuit the request pipeline by omitting next.Invoke or using Run, returning a terminal response before downstream middleware runs.
avoid_when: The failure must carry a reason through the type system: use Result, Either or Option so a caller cannot ignore it, instead of a bare return null.
Validation is genuinely deferred to the point of use (Deferred Validation): drafts, imports and historical records are allowed to exist incomplete, so rejecting at the door is the wrong time.
The checks must accumulate into a violation set (form and batch validation): an error accumulator or a validation pipeline reports every failure at once, while guards report only the first.
The same admission band would repeat across a whole layer: centralise it in an intercepting validator or framework middleware rather than copying guards into every handler.
The function is a one-liner or the condition is the actual work: an if/else expression that returns one of two values is already flat, and a guard would add a second exit without removing nesting.
anti_patterns: Guards with side effects: the check branch logs, mutates or acquires so the 'rejection' performs work; the exit should be a pure divergence.
Copy-pasted validation bands: the same null and range checks in every method of a layer, drifting apart until one copy fails open.
Sentinel returns as failure: returning null, 0 or -1 and hoping every caller checks - a failure without a reason and without a type.
Compound negated guards: if (!(a && !b)) return; - unreadable De Morgan puzzles instead of a named predicate helper.
Guard theatre: a check that catches and swallows (log and continue), so the invalid value flows into the body anyway.
Guarding the impossible: asserting conditions the type system or caller contract already guarantees, padding every function with noise.
design_principles: Fail fast: reject at the earliest point where the failure is detectable and the caller can still act on it.
Separation of concerns: admission checks are separated from the processing that follows them.
Single responsibility per guard: one requirement per exit, named after the requirement rather than the mechanism.
KISS and readability: flat is better than nested; the happy path is the default path.
Design by contract: preconditions are stated explicitly - require, precondition, assert, ThrowIfNull - at the point they are enforced.
best_practices: State each guard as one requirement and exit with the failure shape the caller expects (exception, Err, None, status code) — a bare sentinel only where the API documents it.
Order guards cheapest-first: nil/null checks before database lookups or I/O, so that early exits never pay the cost of an expensive operation they reject.
Keep guard bodies side-effect free; if a guard must log, log and exit without changing shared state.

Extract compound or repeated guards into named predicates — isValidAmount(amount), hasRequiredRole(user, role) — so each guard reads as a named requirement and the predicate is independently testable.
Include the failing value in error messages: 'amount must be positive, got {amount}' rather than 'invalid amount', so failure messages are actionable without replay.
Use the language's contract facility (assert, precondition, debug_assert) for programmer errors; use explicit checks for caller-controlled input — never assert for input that a caller can produce.
Route every exit path through a defined cleanup mechanism (defer, finally, goto-chain) when resources are held; never let a guard exit bypass release of an acquired handle.
When guards multiply beyond three or four, extract the admission band as one validate() helper or delegate to a boundary validator instead of letting the guard block grow.

In async and structured-concurrency contexts, place cancellation checks as early guards before any await; use structured scopes (TaskGroup, scope.run) so child tasks are cancelled when the guard exits.

Use INFO log level for expected invalid-input rejections, WARN for suspicious patterns (repeated bad values from one caller), and ERROR only when a guard detects an internally impossible state — this distinction aids alerting.
Do not repeat the guard inside the body; after the rejection the value is trusted, and the guard is its single check.

In TypeScript, prefer inline structural guards (if (!x) return) over user-defined type predicates for simple non-null checks, as user-defined guards can silently widen return types and break narrowing.

pitfalls: A guard that performs work before the exit — mutating, acquiring, logging state — makes the rejection observable and leaves the caller with a half-applied change.
Negated compound conditions invert the logic twice: name the requirement and test one simple expression, never a De Morgan puzzle.
Duplicated guards drift: the same precondition checked in callers and callee eventually disagrees; keep one owner for the check.

Multiple exit points without defer/finally: a long function with many guards becomes a list of diverging branches, and teams that rely on single-exit discipline for cleanup must route every exit through the same release path or leak resources (CERT MEM12-C documents this exact leak pattern in C).

Silent exits hide errors: a guard that returns a default (null, None, 0, empty collection) turns an invalid input into an ordinary-looking result and discards the reason; when failure must travel with the value, Result/Either/Option carry it and the guard is the wrong shape.

Position matters more than the check: validating early against state that changes before use creates time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) gaps, while validating late lets work happen before the rejection.

Readability can invert: in a function whose guards outnumber its work the code reads as mostly error handling, at which point extraction (Composed Method) or one dedicated validation step is the honest fix.

Guard in async and structured-concurrency contexts: awaiting inside a guard that then throws can leave orphaned child tasks running if the guard exits before the await completes. Use structured scopes (TaskGroup, scope.run) or cancellation tokens so the guard exit cancels in-flight async work.

Type narrowing confusion in TypeScript: a guard `if (!x) return` followed by use of x does NOT narrow x in all paths — user-defined type guard functions can silently widen their return type, and casting inside a guard creates a separate value that TypeScript cannot flow-narrow back to the original. Use inline structural checks or explicit type predicates tested against the specific narrowing failure modes.

Middleware guard ordering: a guard that short-circuits by returning a Response must finalise headers before any streaming begins; returning a Response and also calling await next() produces a double-response error. Each stage must call next() at most once.

Wrong move: add a guard for every small branch in a multi-responsibility method -> the top-of-function validation tree obscures the work and inflates one callable -> instead extract a validator or split the method (Common Mistakes With Guard Clause Pattern).
